title: Custom Food Packaging for Restaurants, Cafes and Bakeries
seoTitle: Custom Food Packaging for Restaurants, Cafes & Bakeries
metaDescription: Branded takeaway packaging that is food-safe, holds up in delivery and keeps costs sensible: boxes, wraps, bags and what to order first.
excerpt: Takeaway and delivery put your packaging in more hands than your dining room ever will. Here is how to choose food-safe, branded packaging that travels well and fits your budget.
coverAlt: Sandwich wrapped in Printy branded butter paper for cafes and restaurants

sections.heading: Your packaging is now part of the meal
sections.body:
For many restaurants, more food leaves in a bag than is eaten at a table. That changes what packaging is for. It is no longer just a container. It is the first thing a delivery customer sees, it sits on their table next to their phone, and it often ends up in a photo.

Plain white boxes do the job, but they are forgettable. Branded packaging turns every order into a small advert for the next one, and it makes your food look like it came from somewhere worth ordering from again.

sections.heading: Start with what your menu needs
sections.body: Before thinking about logos, look at the food itself. Is it hot or cold? Dry, saucy or oily? Eaten on the go or at home? The answers decide the material and the style.
sections.tableCaption: Matching food packaging to menu items
sections.table:
Menu item | Packaging that works | Why
Burgers and sandwiches | Burger box or clamshell, plus wrap paper | Holds shape, wrap stops sauce reaching the box
Fries and fried food | Greaseproof bags, scoops or trays | Oil resistance keeps hands and bags clean
Pizza | Corrugated pizza box | Stiff, stackable, lets steam escape through vents
Cakes and pastries | Bakery box with window | Shows the product, protects decoration
Cookies and donuts | Tray with sleeve or window box | Keeps pieces apart and looks good on display
Salads and bowls | Kraft bowl with lid or folding food box | Leak resistant, easy to eat from

sections.heading: Food safety is not optional
sections.body:
Anything that touches food has to be made from food-grade materials and printed with food-safe inks. In the USA, paper and board in contact with food fall under FDA food contact rules. In the UK and EU the reference is regulation EC 1935/2004.

In practice this means two things. First, ask your supplier to confirm in writing that the board and inks are suitable for food contact. Second, keep heavy printing on the outside of boxes, and use a wrap or liner between very oily food and the box.

For hot, greasy food, a PE (polyethylene) or water-based coating on the inside of the board stops grease from soaking through and weakening the box. Ask which coating is used, as some cities and customers now prefer plastic-free options.

sections.heading: Build a set, not a single box
sections.body:
The strongest food brands look the same across every item: the box, the wrap, the bag and the cup. It does not have to be expensive. A simple system works well:

One or two brand colours used everywhere.

A repeating logo pattern for wraps and bags (cheaper than full artwork).

A larger logo on the lid of the main box, where it is seen and photographed.

A short line or QR code that sends people to your menu or reviews.

Start with the item you sell most, usually the main box or wrap, and add the rest as orders grow.

sections.heading: Delivery tests packaging harder than your counter
sections.body:
A box that is fine for walking to a table can fail after twenty minutes in a delivery bag. A few checks before you order in bulk:

Steam. Hot food creates condensation. Vents or a slightly looser lid stop fries and buns going soggy.

Stacking. Riders stack orders. Corrugated board and flat lids survive this much better than thin folding carton.

Leaks. Sauces need their own pots, and wet dishes need a bowl with a snug lid.

Closing. A tuck lock or a branded sticker keeps the box closed and shows it has not been opened.

sections.heading: Keeping the cost under control
sections.body:
Food packaging is used once and thrown away, so price per unit matters more than for almost any other packaging. Ways to keep it sensible:

Order the most-used sizes in larger quantities. Price per piece drops a lot as quantity rises.

Use one or two print colours. Full colour is rarely needed for food boxes.

Choose standard sizes where you can. Custom sizes are possible, but standard dies are cheaper.

Skip lamination on items that are thrown away within an hour. A clean one-colour print looks professional without it.

sections.heading: Getting a quote for your menu
sections.body:
Send us a list of the items you want to package, roughly how many of each you use in a month, and your logo. We will suggest the right box or wrap for each item and reply with prices and free dielines, usually within an hour during business hours.

Minimum orders start from 100 boxes, production is about 12 to 15 business days after proof approval, and we ship to the USA, UK, Europe, UAE and Australia.

faqs.question: Is printed food packaging safe for direct contact with food?
faqs.answer: Yes, when it is made from food-grade board and printed with food-safe inks. Ask your supplier to confirm compliance with FDA food contact rules in the US or EC 1935/2004 in the UK and EU.

faqs.question: What packaging is best for food delivery?
faqs.answer: Corrugated or coated board boxes with vents for hot food, leak-resistant bowls with lids for wet dishes, and greaseproof wraps or bags for fried items. They handle stacking and steam far better than thin cartons.

faqs.question: Can I order different food boxes in one order?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many restaurants order a set, for example burger boxes, wrap paper and paper bags together, so the whole takeaway order matches.

faqs.question: How can I lower the cost of branded food packaging?
faqs.answer: Use one or two print colours, stick to standard sizes where possible, skip lamination on single-use items, and order your most-used sizes in larger quantities.
